food.text: Between 2500 BCE and 1400 BCE, Saharan agropastoralists known as the Kintampo people settled in what is now Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Togo. They introduced farming and herding to a region that had previously been home only to hunter-gatherers.

In the Sahel zone of northern Mali, domesticated pearl millet was already being grown between 2500 and 2000 BCE, according to archaeobotanical research. This region is considered pearl millet's center of diversity and likely place of first domestication.

Between 1500 and 900 BCE, Nok peoples migrating into central Nigeria brought with them the knowledge of cultivating tamed pearl millet. This introduced one of Africa's oldest grain crops to the region.

Charred cowpea remains found in rock shelters in central Ghana have been dated to the second millennium BCE. The cowpea is considered one of the oldest crops to be farmed, valued for its tolerance to sandy soil and low rainfall.

The Kintampo people cultivated pearl millet, a crop well suited to hot climates, and may have deliberately bred it to mature faster so it could be harvested more quickly. This adaptation would have helped early West African farmers cope with the region's growing conditions.

One of the earliest known sites of pearl millet farming in West Africa is Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania, where remains have been dated to between 1936 and 1683 BCE. This makes it among the earliest known evidence of pearl millet cultivation in Africa.

Archaeological evidence points to a distinct shift toward food production in the West African forest zone between about 3,600 and 3,200 years ago. This change is linked to the arrival of Saharan-derived farming peoples such as those of the Kintampo tradition.

Charred pearl millet remains excavated at Kintampo sites show the grain could be stored after harvest and used later. This storability made pearl millet especially valuable to Bronze Age communities in West Africa.

Archaeologists found Kintampo pearl millet alongside shell beads imported from the ocean, evidence that these Bronze Age farmers traded food and goods across the region. Such finds show pearl millet farmers were connected to distant coastal trade networks.

At Dhar Tichitt and Dhar Walata in Mauritania, pearl millet may have been independently tamed during the Neolithic. These sites belong to the Tichitt Tradition, whose culture included the farming of cereals.

art.text: In eastern Mauritania, the Tichitt Tradition lasted from 2200 BCE to 200 BCE. Its people built dry stonewalled architecture at sites such as Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Walata and Dhar Néma. Such walls persisted there between 1900 BCE and 400 BCE.

"Seated" and "crouched" chimpanzee statuettes developed between 2300 BCE and 1500 BCE. Speculatively, such artistic depictions may have been traded over long distances from West Africa or Central Africa into the Near East, for example to Elam.

In the Sahelian region of West Africa, the Tichitt Tradition developed corded roulette ceramics. These pots persisted alongside dry stonewalled architecture in Mauritania between 1900 BCE and 400 BCE, at places such as Dhar Tichitt and Dhar Tagant.

By 2000 BCE, as aridification followed the Holocene Climate Optimum, Tichitt pastoralists had become agropastoralists. Their economy combined herding, millet farming and stonemasonry, which included architecture, in the settlement areas of Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Walata and Dhar Néma.

The stone-walled Tichitt settlements varied greatly in scale, from 2 hectares to 80 hectares. Within them were walled agricultural land used for livestock or gardening, as well as land with granaries and tumuli.

One speculative route for the chimpanzee statuettes ran by maritime trade from the Gulf of Guinea to the eastern Mediterranean, along the Incense Route and into the Near East. This idea comes via the report of Hanno the Navigator.

war.text: Between about 2600 and 1200 BC, West Africa developed an iron industry used for both smelting and forging. This early ironworking supplied both tools and weapons, marking one of the region's earliest advances in war-related technology.

Across Mauritania, the Tichitt tradition built one of West Africa's earliest known systems of walled settlements. Dry stone architecture appeared at sites such as Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Walata, Dhar Néma and Dhar Tagant between about 1900 BCE and 400 BCE.
At Dhar Tichitt itself, some settlements were further enclosed by large stone circumvallation walls. Construction of the plateau's walled compounds began as early as 1400 BCE.
These stone walls at Tichitt tradition sites varied enormously in scale, from about 2 hectares up to 80 hectares. They enclosed farmland, granaries and burial tumuli within the fortified settlements.

literature.text: Nsibidi, a West African script, may have developed as early as 5000 BCE, though it may date to 2000 BCE. The evidence is its depiction on the Ikom monoliths at Ikom, in Nigeria.
The Nsibidi script may have developed by 2000 BCE, as shown by depictions of it on Ikom monoliths at Ikom in Nigeria. Some suggest it may have developed as early as 5000 BCE.

science.text: In the Aïr Mountains region of Niger, copper was independently smelted between 3000 BCE and 2500 BCE. The smelting quality was not well developed, which indicates the technique was not introduced from an external region such as the Nile Valley.

Iron ironworking did more than make better tools. It improved weaponry and let farmers expand agricultural productivity and produce surplus crops, which together supported the growth of urban city-states into empires.
Niger-Congo speakers in West Africa domesticated the helmeted guineafowl sometime between 5500 and 1300 years ago.
One of the earliest known sites of ironworking in West Africa is Lejja, in southeastern Nigeria. Researchers Bandama and Babalola dated its iron smelting furnaces to as early as 2631 to 2458 BCE.
Excavations in the Nsukka region of southeast Nigeria, in what is now Igboland, found iron smelting furnaces and slag. At the site of Lejja they date to 2000 BC, while those at Opi date to 750 BC.

In the Aïr Mountains, the quality of the copper smelting process became more developed by 1500 BCE. This suggests local smelters refined their technique over roughly a thousand years after first smelting copper.

Earlier research by Eze-Uzomaka in 2009 had dated Lejja's iron smelting furnaces to about 2000 BC. A 2023 study by Bandama and Babalola later pushed the site's earliest ironworking further back, to between 2631 and 2458 BCE.

Iron furnaces and slag at Lejja in southeast Nigeria's Igboland have been dated to 2000 BC. At Opi, a nearby site, similar remains date to 750 BC. Together they suggest iron metallurgy may have been developed independently in West Africa.

Bandama and Babalola (2023) indicated that iron metallurgical development at Lejja in Nigeria occurred between 2631 BCE and 2458 BCE. That is among the earliest dates proposed for ironworking anywhere in West Africa.

Bandama and Babalola (2023) also dated iron metallurgical development at Tchire Ouma 147 in Niger to between 1895 BCE and 1370 BCE. At Dekpassanware in Togo, they dated it to between 1297 BCE and 1051 BCE.

Iron metallurgical development has been dated at Lejja in Nigeria to between 2631 BCE and 2458 BCE, and at Dekpassanware in Togo to between 1297 BCE and 1051 BCE. These archaeometallurgical developments are considered native African technologies.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Iron metallurgical development also reached Tchire Ouma 147, in Niger, by between 1895 and 1370 BCE. This dating comes from the same 2023 study by Bandama and Babalola, showing how early ironworking spread across parts of West Africa.

politics.text: By 2200 BCE, the Tichitt Tradition of eastern Mauritania had developed a four-tiered hierarchical social structure across the settlements of Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Néma, Dhar Tagant, and Dhar Walata. This makes it one of the earliest known examples of complex social organization in West Africa.

In the Hodh Depression of southern Mauritania, pastoralist communities began developing early forms of pre-state urbanism starting in the early 2nd millennium BCE. Their settlements showed patterns of nucleation and social differentiation, marking a shift toward more organized political life.

In the Kintampo complex of what is now Ghana, Saharan-derived agropastoralists arrived between 2500 and 1400 BCE among existing hunter-gatherer foragers. Their arrival introduced new social differentiation to a landscape that had previously been organized without such hierarchy.

Dhar Tichitt, including the site of Dakhlet el Atrouss, may have served as the primary regional center governing the hierarchical social structure of the wider Tichitt Tradition. This positions it as a central hub within one of West Africa's earliest complex societies.

Social stratification among the Saharan pastoralists who formed the Tichitt Tradition is evidenced by lavish grave goods, including beads, bracelets, hachettes, and lustrous stone axes, found buried within funerary tumuli. Such items suggest that status and wealth were unevenly distributed among community members.

By 1800 BCE, the sophisticated social hierarchies first developed among Saharan cattle-herders had spread throughout the Saharan and Sahelian regions. This expansion helped lay the groundwork for the stratified settlements later built at Dhar Tichitt.

Some settlements of the Tichitt Tradition were enclosed by large communal stone 'circumvallation walls', with livestock enclosures built nearby. This kind of coordinated construction points to organized communal decision-making within the tradition's hierarchical settlements.

Mandé-speaking peoples, ancestors of the Soninke, migrated from the Central Sahara and established the Tichitt culture in Mauritania. Dhar Tichitt served as its primary regional center, with the Malian Lakes Region possibly acting as a secondary one.

Walled settlements of the Tichitt Tradition varied enormously in scale, from as small as 2 hectares to as large as 80 hectares. Within their stone walls lay agricultural land for livestock and gardening, alongside granaries and funerary tumuli.

culture.text: The Nok culture takes its name from the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, Nigeria, where its terracotta sculptures were first found in 1928. Nok culture may have emerged in 1500 BCE and persisted until 1 BCE.

Excluding ancient Egyptian figurative art, Nok sculptures are regarded as the earliest large three-dimensional figurative art in continental Africa. Later West African artistic traditions, such as Ile Ife of Nigeria, may have been shaped by this earlier clay terracotta tradition.
As of 3500 years ago, Nok agriculturalists gathered bee products, including honey collected in pottery. The honey may have been added to West African cuisines.

The Nok people and the Gajiganna people may have migrated from the Central Sahara, along with pearl millet and pottery. They may have diverged before arriving in northern Nigeria, leading to settlements in the regions of Gajiganna and Nok.
Some Nok terracotta sculptures portray figures wielding slingshots, as well as bows and arrows. This may indicate that Nok people hunted or trapped undomesticated animals.
A Nok sculpture shows two individuals, along with their goods, in a dugout canoe, both paddling. It may indicate that Nok people used dugout canoes to transport cargo along tributaries.
Beeswax and animal fats found as remnants on Nok ceramics suggest the pottery was used to store meat. Honey may have been used for preservation purposes.
